case_studies.title: Beyond Predictable Paths: Redefining AI Security Incident Reporting for Agents
case_studies.abstract: AI agents are being deployed rapidly, accompanied by a growing number of AI-specific attacks and corresponding incidents. As incident reporting becomes increasingly important for legal compliance, governance, accountability, and security; current frameworks must be adapted to the unique characteristics of AI agents. In this paper, two editorial authors compare AI systems and AI agents and, drawing on input from 23 experts in academia and industry, identify the information required for reporting incidents where the security of AI agents is harmed. %involving AI agents. Potential reporting eleme
case_studies.summary: The paper outlines what data should be captured when an AI agent is attacked, highlighting that current incident-reporting standards miss key AI‑specific details. The authors surveyed 23 experts and produced a checklist of information needed for compliant AI‑agent incident reports. The result is a proposed framework that could help organisations meet legal and governance requirements when securing AI agents.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure that hosts AI agents, here is what to do: 1) Update your incident‑reporting templates to include the AI‑agent‑specific fields identified in the paper (e.g., model version, data sources, and agent behaviour logs). 2) Train your security teams to capture and log these fields during any incident. 3) Verify compliance with the new framework before reporting to regulators or clients.
case_studies.score_reasoning: Novelty 20 – provides a new framework for AI‑agent incident reporting that is not widely known among IT ops professionals. IT relevance 25 – directly addresses security, compliance, and governance issues that affect infrastructure teams using AI agents. Value_90_Days 30 – offers concrete reporting elements and expert inputs that can be implemented in existing incident management workflows within three months. Overall high score, no low_signal.

case_studies.title: Structured Decomposition for Reliable LLM-Generated Access Control Policies
case_studies.abstract: This paper presents an LLM-based system that translates natural-language access control policies (NLACPs) into executable Rego code for Open Policy Agent (OPA). It provides a modular, end-to-end pipeline for policy detection, component extraction, schema validation, linting, compilation, and automated test generation and execution. The system is designed to bridge the gap between human-readable access requirements and machine-enforceable policy-as-code (PaC), with a focus on deployment reliability and security correctness. We evaluate the system on 372 ACRE-complete access control statements w
case_studies.summary: This research introduces a tool that turns natural‑language access control rules into Rego code for OPA, with automatic validation and test generation to ensure reliability. It builds a full pipeline that detects policies, extracts components, checks against schemas, lints, compiles, and runs tests. The result is higher confidence that the policies you deploy are correct and secure.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage OPA in your cloud, 1) feed your NLACPs to the tool to auto‑generate Rego, 2) run the built‑in tests to confirm correctness, 3) merge the output into your CI/CD pipeline for continuous validation.

case_studies.title: When the Agent Becomes the Kernel: A Systematization of Security on the Path to AI-Native Operating Systems
case_studies.abstract: Large language model agents are now privileged principals that take consequential actions: editing code repositories, operating inboxes, completing purchases. Their authority is kernel-grade, but it comes without what classical systems security requires: a trusted mediator interposed on every access. Operating-system vendors are now rebuilding the platform around this de-facto agent kernel, inheriting complete mediation as a design problem. We systematize the security of such systems around a single distinction: a crossing mediated over provenance admits a deterministic check, while one over c
case_studies.summary: Large‑language‑model agents now act like operating‑system kernels, making changes to code, mail, and purchases without a trusted mediator. The authors propose a security framework that ensures any agent action is mediated by a provenance check, giving a deterministic way to verify trust. The result is a set of design principles that could guide the creation of AI‑native OSes and similar systems.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure, check whether your automated agents (e.g., CI/CD pipelines, auto‑scaling scripts, AI‑assistants) perform all privileged actions through a provenance‑based mediator; if not, add a layer that records and validates each agent’s action history before execution. This flags a risk: if your organisation uses any AI‑powered automation without such checks, immediately audit for unmediated access paths.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper addresses security in AI‑native operating systems, a topic that is novel and directly relevant to IT engineers managing infrastructure. It proposes a framework for mediated access that can inform security policies around agent‑based systems. While the concepts are actionable, the immediate applicability is limited to security‑focused teams, so the value for quick deployment is moderate.

case_studies.title: One to More, More to One: Category-Aware Iterative Expert Training for Software Engineering Agents
case_studies.abstract: Repository-level software engineering (SWE) comprises heterogeneous task categories, whose progress under pooled agentic reinforcement learning can be uneven: gains in some categories coincide with regressions in others, while aggregate resolution obscures these changes. Motivated by this category see-saw, we develop a category-aware expert-training and policy-integration framework. Executable task construction and SWE Labeler, an evidence-grounded multi-axis labeling system, organize the training pools. Initial category-specific RL improves average training success while leaving uneven instan
case_studies.summary: The study tackles uneven performance across different software engineering task categories when using reinforcement learning agents. It introduces a category‑aware training framework, including a task construction tool and an evidence‑based labeling system, which together raise overall training success rates. This is directly relevant for IT teams that deploy AI agents in multi‑domain development workflows.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud‑based AI agents for software engineering, step 1: identify the task categories your agents handle and note any performance dips. Step 2: integrate a category‑aware training pipeline that isolates and trains on each category separately, using a label system to validate results. Step 3: merge the specialised policies back into your main agent and monitor for improved, balanced performance across all categories.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper introduces a category-aware iterative training framework for reinforcement learning agents in software engineering, which could inform future automation tools. However, it lacks immediate actionable steps for infrastructure or SaaS tooling, and practical deployment within 90 days is unlikely.
